CALIFORNIA WARN ACT (CAL/WARN) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

WHETHER THIS NOTICE IS REQUIRED
California has its own layoff-notice law — the California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act, commonly called "Cal/WARN" — separate from the federal WARN Act. It applies to Acme Corp only if Acme Corp operates a "covered establishment": a facility that employs, or has employed at any point in the preceding 12 months, 75 or more people. That threshold is lower than federal WARN's 100-employee threshold, and the California statute's definition doesn't exclude part-time workers the way the federal one does. An "employer" under this law is whoever directly or indirectly owns and operates that covered establishment — including a parent corporation, as to a covered establishment owned and operated by its subsidiary. And a covered "employee" — the person to whom the liability described elsewhere in this document can run — is someone who has worked for the employer at least 6 of the 12 months before the date notice would be due.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Covered establishment” means any industrial or commercial facility or part thereof that employs, or has employed within the preceding 12 months, 75 or more persons."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "covered establishment" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  "“Employer” means any person, as defined by Section 18, who directly or indirectly owns and operates a covered establishment. A parent corporation is an employer as to any covered establishment directly owned and operated by its corporate subsidiary."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "employer" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  "“Employee” means a person employed by an employer for at least 6 months of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(h) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "employee" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  Known gap: The three quotes below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1400.5) rather than independently authored sources, so they aren't cross-corroborated against each other. Separately: Labor Code § 1400.5(b) defines "employer" by cross-referencing the general "person" definition in Labor Code § 18; that cross-referenced section wasn't independently fetched and verified for this document, so this clause states the covered-establishment/employer/employee definitions only as directly written in § 1400.5 itself.

WHAT COUNTS AS A MASS LAYOFF, RELOCATION, OR TERMINATION
Cal/WARN's notice duty is triggered by three distinct events at a covered establishment: a "mass layoff" — a layoff of 50 or more employees during any 30-day period — a "relocation" — moving all or substantially all of the covered establishment's operations 100 or more miles away — or a "termination" — ceasing or substantially ceasing operations there. Unlike the federal mass-layoff definition, California's has no separate test tied to what percentage of the workforce is affected; a flat count of 50 or more employees within 30 days is enough regardless of how large the covered establishment's total workforce is. The chapter also carves out two situations entirely: layoffs from the completion of a project-based job in the broadcasting, motion picture, or certain on-site construction/drilling/logging/mining industries where the employee understood the job was tied to that project, and layoffs of employees hired with the understanding that the work was seasonal and temporary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Mass layoff” means a layoff during any 30-day period of 50 or more employees at a covered establishment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "mass layoff" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  "“Relocation” means the removal of all or substantially all of the industrial or commercial operations in a covered establishment to a different location 100 miles or more away."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(e)-(f) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "relocation" and "termination" definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  "“Termination” means the cessation or substantial cessation of industrial or commercial operations in a covered establishment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(f) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "termination" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  "(g) (1) This chapter does not apply where the closing or layoff is the result of the completion of a particular project or undertaking of an employer subject to Wage Order 11, regulating the Broadcasting Industry, Wage Order 12, regulating the Motion Picture Industry, or Wage Order 16, regulating Certain On-Site Occupations in the Construction, Drilling, Logging and Mining Industries, of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and the employees were hired with the understanding that their employment was limited to the duration of that project or undertaking. (2) This chapter does not apply to employees who are employed in seasonal employment where the employees were hired with the understanding that their employment was seasonal and temporary."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(g) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, project-based and seasonal-employment carve-outs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1400.5.)
  Known gap: All quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1400.5) rather than independently authored sources. This clause also doesn't address Cal/WARN's separate call-center-relocation article (Labor Code §§ 1409-1413), which applies its own relocation definition to call centers specifically and was outside the scope of this document's research.

THE 60-DAY NOTICE REQUIREMENT AND WHAT IT MUST CONTAIN
If the thresholds above are met, California law requires Acme Corp to give written notice at least 60 days before November 1, 2026, the date the mass layoff, relocation, or termination is expected to take effect. Notice goes not only to Jordan Alex Lee and the other affected employees, but also to the Employment Development Department, the local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government where the event will occur. The notice itself has to include everything the federal WARN Act requires, plus several California-specific items: a functioning email and phone number for the local workforce development board along with a required description of that board's rapid-response services (this applies regardless of whether Acme Corp plans to coordinate with the board or with someone else), a description of the CalFresh food-assistance program with its benefits helpline and a link to the CalFresh website, and a functioning email and phone number for Acme Corp itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer may not order a mass layoff, relocation, or termination at a covered establishment unless, 60 days before the order takes effect, the employer gives written notice of the order to the following: (1) The employees of the covered establishment affected by the order. (2) The Employment Development Department, the local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government within which the termination, relocation, or mass layoff occurs."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1401(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, 60-day notice requirement and recipients (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1401.)
  "An employer required to give notice of any mass layoff, relocation, or termination under this chapter shall include in its notice the elements required by the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2101 et seq.)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1401(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, incorporation of federal notice elements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1401.)
  "Regardless of whether the employer chooses to coordinate services with the local workforce development board or another entity, the employer shall include in the notice a functioning email and telephone number of the board and the following description of the rapid response activities offered by the local workforce development board"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1401(c)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, required rapid-response-service disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1401.)
  "An employer required to give notice of any mass layoff, relocation, or termination under this chapter shall include in the notice a description of the statewide food assistance program known as CalFresh (Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 18900) of Part 6 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code), the CalFresh benefits helpline, and a link to the CalFresh internet website."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1401(d)-(e) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, required CalFresh and employer-contact disclosures (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1401.)
  Known gap: The four citations below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1401) rather than independently authored sources. Section 1401(c)(2) separately requires that if the employer does choose to coordinate rapid-response services through the workforce board or another entity, those services be arranged within 30 days of the notice — a scheduling duty this clause doesn't restate in full. This document doesn't separately verify or reproduce the exact wording the federal WARN Act itself requires notices to contain; see this project's federal WARN Act document for that.

WHEN NOTICE ISN'T REQUIRED
California law recognizes two situations where the 60-day notice described above isn't required. First, no notice at all is required if the mass layoff, relocation, or termination is necessitated by a physical calamity or act of war. Second, an employer need not comply with the notice requirement for a relocation or termination — not a mass layoff — if the state Employment Development Department determines that the employer was actively and in good faith seeking capital or business that, if obtained, would have let it avoid or postpone the relocation or termination, and that the employer reasonably believed giving notice would have prevented it from getting that capital or business. That second exception isn't self-executing the way its closest federal counterpart is: before it applies, the employer has to give the department a written record of the documents relevant to that determination, along with an affidavit — signed under penalty of perjury — verifying the record's contents. Cal/WARN does not have a standalone exception for generic "unforeseeable business circumstances" the way federal WARN does.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding the requirements of subdivision (a), an employer is not required to provide notice if a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is necessitated by a physical calamity or act of war."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1401(f) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, physical-calamity/act-of-war exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1401.)
  "An employer is not required to comply with the notice requirement contained in subdivision (a) of Section 1401 if the department determines that all of the following conditions exist: (1) As of the time that notice would have been required, the employer was actively seeking capital or business. (2) The capital or business sought, if obtained, would have enabled the employer to avoid or postpone the relocation or termination. (3) The employer reasonably and in good faith believed that giving the notice required by subdivision (a) of Section 1401 would have precluded the employer from obtaining the needed capital or business."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, active-seeking-capital-or-business exception and its procedural conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.5.)
  "The department may not determine that the employer was actively seeking capital or business under subdivision (a) unless the employer provides the department with both of the following: (1) A written record consisting of all documents relevant to the determination of whether the employer was actively seeking capital or business, as specified by the department. (2) An affidavit verifying the contents of the documents contained in the record."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, written-record and sworn-affidavit conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.5.)
  "This section does not apply to notice of a mass layoff as defined by subdivision (d) of Section 1400."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, exclusion of mass layoffs from the active-seeking-capital exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.5.)
  Known gap: Labor Code § 1402.5(d) — the provision stating the active-seeking-capital exception doesn't apply to mass layoffs — refers to a mass-layoff definition at "subdivision (d) of Section 1400." As currently published, however, Section 1400 contains only the Act's short title and has no lettered subdivisions; the mass-layoff definition this document found is instead at subdivision (d) of Section 1400.5. This appears to be an uncorrected cross-reference left over from a 2022 amendment that renumbered the definitions out of Section 1400 and into a new Section 1400.5 without updating this particular internal citation. This clause treats § 1402.5(d)'s carve-out as referring to the current mass-layoff definition despite that stale section number, but does not independently resolve the discrepancy. Separately, the two citations below come from two different statutory sections (§ 1401(f) and § 1402.5), so they are independent of each other within the same chapter.

WHAT HAPPENS IF NOTICE ISN'T GIVEN — EMPLOYEE LIABILITY
An employer that orders a mass layoff, relocation, or termination without giving employees the notice described above is liable to each employee who lost their job and was entitled to notice for back pay — at the higher of the employee's average regular rate over their last three years of employment or their final rate of compensation — plus the value of any benefits, including medical expenses, the employee would have received had the employment loss not happened. This liability runs for the period of the violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or half the number of days the employee actually worked for the employer, whichever is smaller. It's reduced by wages the employer actually paid during the violation period (except accrued vacation pay), any voluntary payment not otherwise legally required, and certain third-party benefit payments made on the employee's behalf.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer who fails to give notice as required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 1401 before ordering a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is liable to each employee entitled to notice who lost his or her employment for: (1) Back pay at the average regular rate of compensation received by the employee during the last three years of his or her employment, or the employee’s final rate of compensation, whichever is higher. (2) The value of the cost of any benefits to which the employee would have been entitled had his or her employment not been lost, including the cost of any medical expenses incurred by the employee that would have been covered under an employee benefit plan."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, back pay and benefits liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.)
  "Liability under this section is calculated for the period of the employer’s violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or one-half the number of days that the employee was employed by the employer, whichever period is smaller."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, liability cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.)
  "The amount of an employer’s liability under subdivision (a) is reduced by the following: (1) Any wages, except vacation moneys accrued prior to the period of the employer’s violation, paid by the employer to the employee during the period of the employer’s violation. (2) Any voluntary and unconditional payments made by the employer to the employee that were not required to satisfy any legal obligation. (3) Any payments by the employer to a third party or trustee, such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan, on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1402(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, offsets against liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1402.)
  Known gap: The three citations below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1402) rather than independently authored sources. This liability formula tracks the structure of the parallel federal WARN Act damages provision closely, but this clause states only the California statute's own text; it doesn't address how an employee's rights under the two statutes for the same layoff relate to each other, which the sections fetched for this document do not say.

GOVERNMENT PENALTY, PRIVATE LAWSUITS, AND STATE ENFORCEMENT
Beyond the per-employee liability described above, an employer that fails to notify the Employment Development Department, local workforce board, and local officials is subject to a civil penalty of up to $500 for each day of the violation — waived if the employer pays everything owed to affected employees within three weeks of ordering the layoff, relocation, or termination. Any person seeking to establish liability against an employer under this chapter, including a local government or an employee representative, may bring a civil action, including on behalf of others similarly situated, and a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing plaintiff. A court may also reduce a penalty if the employer shows it conducted a reasonable, good-faith investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation. Separately from any private lawsuit, California's Labor Commissioner has independent authority to examine an employer's books and records and to enforce the notice requirement directly — including by investigating a violation, ordering temporary relief, and issuing a citation against the employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer who fails to give notice as required by paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 1401 is subject to a civil penalty of not more than five hundred dollars ($500) for each day of the employer’s violation. The employer is not subject to a civil penalty under this section, however, if the employer pays to all applicable employees the amounts for which the employer is liable under Section 1402 within three weeks from the date the employer orders the mass layoff, relocation, or termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1403 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, civil penalty for failing to notify government recipients (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1403.)
  "A person, including a local government or an employee representative, seeking to establish liability against an employer may bring a civil action on behalf of the person, other persons similarly situated, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction. The court may award reasonable attorney’s fees as part of costs to any plaintiff who prevails in a civil action brought under this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1404 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, private civil action and attorney's fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1404.)
  "If the court determines that an employer conducted a reasonable investigation in good faith, and had reasonable grounds to believe that its conduct was not a violation of this chapter, the court may reduce the amount of any penalty imposed against the employer under this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1405 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, good-faith reduction of penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1405.)
  "In any investigation or proceeding under this chapter, the Labor Commissioner has, in addition to all other powers granted by law, the authority to examine the books and records of an employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1406(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, Labor Commissioner investigation and citation authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1406.)
  Known gap: The four citations below come from four different statutory sections (§§ 1403, 1404, 1405, and 1406), so they are independently drawn from separate parts of the chapter rather than repeated subdivisions of one section. The $500-per-day civil penalty described first is tied specifically to a failure to notify the government recipients under Labor Code § 1401(a)(2) — the Employment Development Department, workforce board, and local officials — not to a failure to notify employees themselves, which is a narrower trigger than it may first appear.

NOTICE OF LAYOFF, RELOCATION, OR TERMINATION
This notice is provided to Jordan Alex Lee by Acme Corp pursuant to the California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act (Cal/WARN Act), Labor Code § 1400 et seq.

Acme Corp anticipates a mass layoff, relocation, or termination affecting Jordan Alex Lee's position, expected to take effect on or about November 1, 2026.

A copy of this notice, or one materially like it, is also being sent to the California Employment Development Department, the applicable local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government where this event will occur, as required by California law.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge receipt of this notice.

Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Date: _______________

(3) The employer reasonably and in good faith believed that giving the notice required by subdivision (a) of Section 1401 would have precluded the employer from obtaining the needed capital or business.

citations.quote: The department may not determine that the employer was actively seeking capital or business under subdivision (a) unless the employer provides the department with both of the following: (1) A written record consisting of all documents relevant to the determination of whether the employer was actively seeking capital or business, as specified by the department. (2) An affidavit verifying the contents of the documents contained in the record.

expectedJSON.gap: Labor Code § 1402.5(d) — the provision stating the active-seeking-capital exception doesn't apply to mass layoffs — refers to a mass-layoff definition at "subdivision (d) of Section 1400." As currently published, however, Section 1400 contains only the Act's short title and has no lettered subdivisions; the mass-layoff definition this document found is instead at subdivision (d) of Section 1400.5. This appears to be an uncorrected cross-reference left over from a 2022 amendment that renumbered the definitions out of Section 1400 and into a new Section 1400.5 without updating this particular internal citation. This clause treats § 1402.5(d)'s carve-out as referring to the current mass-layoff definition despite that stale section number, but does not independently resolve the discrepancy. Separately, the two citations below come from two different statutory sections (§ 1401(f) and § 1402.5), so they are independent of each other within the same chapter.

expectedJSON.body: An employer that orders a mass layoff, relocation, or termination without giving employees the notice described above is liable to each employee who lost their job and was entitled to notice for back pay — at the higher of the employee's average regular rate over their last three years of employment or their final rate of compensation — plus the value of any benefits, including medical expenses, the employee would have received had the employment loss not happened. This liability runs for the period of the violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or half the number of days the employee actually worked for the employer, whichever is smaller. It's reduced by wages the employer actually paid during the violation period (except accrued vacation pay), any voluntary payment not otherwise legally required, and certain third-party benefit payments made on the employee's behalf.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(a) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, back pay and benefits liability
citations.quote: An employer who fails to give notice as required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 1401 before ordering a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is liable to each employee entitled to notice who lost his or her employment for: (1) Back pay at the average regular rate of compensation received by the employee during the last three years of his or her employment, or the employee’s final rate of compensation, whichever is higher. (2) The value of the cost of any benefits to which the employee would have been entitled had his or her employment not been lost, including the cost of any medical expenses incurred by the employee that would have been covered under an employee benefit plan.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, liability cap
citations.quote: Liability under this section is calculated for the period of the employer’s violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or one-half the number of days that the employee was employed by the employer, whichever period is smaller.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, offsets against liability
citations.quote: The amount of an employer’s liability under subdivision (a) is reduced by the following: (1) Any wages, except vacation moneys accrued prior to the period of the employer’s violation, paid by the employer to the employee during the period of the employer’s violation. (2) Any voluntary and unconditional payments made by the employer to the employee that were not required to satisfy any legal obligation. (3) Any payments by the employer to a third party or trustee, such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan, on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation.

expectedJSON.gap: The three citations below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1402) rather than independently authored sources. This liability formula tracks the structure of the parallel federal WARN Act damages provision closely, but this clause states only the California statute's own text; it doesn't address how an employee's rights under the two statutes for the same layoff relate to each other, which the sections fetched for this document do not say.

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the per-employee liability described above, an employer that fails to notify the Employment Development Department, local workforce board, and local officials is subject to a civil penalty of up to $500 for each day of the violation — waived if the employer pays everything owed to affected employees within three weeks of ordering the layoff, relocation, or termination. Any person seeking to establish liability against an employer under this chapter, including a local government or an employee representative, may bring a civil action, including on behalf of others similarly situated, and a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing plaintiff. A court may also reduce a penalty if the employer shows it conducted a reasonable, good-faith investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation. Separately from any private lawsuit, California's Labor Commissioner has independent authority to examine an employer's books and records and to enforce the notice requirement directly — including by investigating a violation, ordering temporary relief, and issuing a citation against the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1403 (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, civil penalty for failing to notify government recipients
citations.quote: An employer who fails to give notice as required by paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 1401 is subject to a civil penalty of not more than five hundred dollars ($500) for each day of the employer’s violation. The employer is not subject to a civil penalty under this section, however, if the employer pays to all applicable employees the amounts for which the employer is liable under Section 1402 within three weeks from the date the employer orders the mass layoff, relocation, or termination.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1404 (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, private civil action and attorney's fees
citations.quote: A person, including a local government or an employee representative, seeking to establish liability against an employer may bring a civil action on behalf of the person, other persons similarly situated, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction. The court may award reasonable attorney’s fees as part of costs to any plaintiff who prevails in a civil action brought under this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1405 (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, good-faith reduction of penalty
citations.quote: If the court determines that an employer conducted a reasonable investigation in good faith, and had reasonable grounds to believe that its conduct was not a violation of this chapter, the court may reduce the amount of any penalty imposed against the employer under this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1406(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, Labor Commissioner investigation and citation authority
citations.quote: In any investigation or proceeding under this chapter, the Labor Commissioner has, in addition to all other powers granted by law, the authority to examine the books and records of an employer.

expectedJSON.gap: The four citations below come from four different statutory sections (§§ 1403, 1404, 1405, and 1406), so they are independently drawn from separate parts of the chapter rather than repeated subdivisions of one section. The $500-per-day civil penalty described first is tied specifically to a failure to notify the government recipients under Labor Code § 1401(a)(2) — the Employment Development Department, workforce board, and local officials — not to a failure to notify employees themselves, which is a narrower trigger than it may first appear.
